# Measuring a synthetic audience panel

**A method for landing, scaling, and reading concept-test data generated by language models — and for telling a real finding apart from an artefact of the instrument.**

ABR / Air Bud Returns · `42p.0.0-ABR-HTR-09-01-1` wave · September 2026

---

## Abstract

Synthetic archetype panels produce survey-shaped data that is not survey data. It arrives wide,
it carries option codes whose direction is not fixed, some of its headline metrics arrive as
prose, and the same construct is asked on different scale lengths in different files. Analysed
with ordinary survey arithmetic it produces numbers that are confidently and specifically
wrong — in the prior wave of this study, an apparent 37 to 54 point collapse in appeal with
age that did not exist.

This paper documents the pipeline built for the ABR concept test: how the data is landed, how
"top box" is decided per question rather than assumed, how semantic and theme analysis is
scoped so that its numbers mean something, and — the part that matters most for a synthetic
panel — how anything is validated at all when there is no human benchmark to calibrate
against.

The central empirical result is a measurement of the panel's own instability. Two
independently generated runs of the same instrument, on disjoint personas, agree well on rank
order (ρ = 0.53–0.69) and move a mean of **6 to 9 latent points on levels**. That number is the
error bar that belongs on every single-run figure this method produces, and it is larger than
any sampling interval in the study.

---

## 1. The data, and why it is not survey data

Each export is one panel of personas, one row each, very wide:

```
46 persona attribute columns │ 34 aat_* diagnostic columns │ N × 7 question columns
archetype_id, gender, age,   │ pre/post interest, pacing,  │ Q{n}_question, Q{n}_meta,
income, psychographics, …    │ polarization, diagnostics   │ Q{n}_type, Q{n}_rating_label,
                             │ JSON, …                     │ Q{n}_rating, Q{n}_selected,
                             │                             │ Q{n}_qual
```

The current wave is three exports:

| Panel | Personas | Questions | Columns | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `HTR_MAIN` | 273 | 83 | 661 | Adults: 188 parents, 85 non-parents |
| `HTR_K9` | 125 | 40 | 360 | Children 7–12 |
| `HTR_K3` | 25 | 36 | 332 | Children 4–6 |

423 personas, 28,559 question-answer facts, 7,277 verbatims. Two earlier exports of a related
instrument (`TSR_T1`, `TSR_T23`; 152 personas) are landed alongside, and their role is
explained in §6.

Three properties make this shape hostile to ordinary analysis, and all three are structural
rather than incidental:

**`Q{n}` is a position, not an identity.** `Q1` in the adult file is a device question; `Q1` in
a children's file is an age question. The stable identity of a question is `(panel, meta,
question_text)`. Any pipeline that keys on position produces a table where columns silently
mean different things in different rows.

**The column count varies by export.** 332, 360 and 661 in this wave. So the reshape cannot be
written once and reused, and a wildcard load across exports either fails on schema mismatch or
discards the provenance that later comparison depends on.

**Answers arrive as English, not as numbers.** `Q*_rating` is empty in 100% of cells in every
export of this study. The quantitative signal is a label string in `Q*_selected`, and for ten
adult metrics there is no closed-end at all — only a sentence.

---

## 2. Six ways the data misleads a careful analyst

Each of these was found by measurement, and each one, left unhandled, produces a specific wrong
number rather than a vague loss of quality.

### 2.1 Option-code direction is not fixed

The current wave codes its closed-ends (`1. I liked it a lot!`), which the prior wave did not.
But the direction varies **within a single file**:

```
Q5  KPLIKE2   1. I liked it a lot!          ← 1 = best
Q6  KPWANT    5. I really want to see it    ← 5 = best, four columns later
```

A global rule of "top box = code 1" reports the bottom box as the top box on roughly half the
battery.

### 2.2 Twenty questions print a second scale number that runs backwards

The adult `POSTATT` and `TREFFECT` batteries look like this:

```
1. 5 – To a very great extent
2. 4 – To a great extent
3. 3 – To a moderate extent
4. 2 – To a small extent
5. 1 – Not at all
```

Two numbers per option, running in opposite directions. The printed point is the
questionnaire's scale; the export code is an artefact of option ordering. 22 questions print a
point and **20 of them disagree with the code**. Ranking by code inverts each one.

### 2.3 Sentinel options sit mid-scale

`I'm not sure` is option code 6 in one question and code 3 in another. The convention inherited
from an earlier study — that sentinels live at codes ≥ 90 — is simply false here. Sentinels can
only be identified by label, and if they are not excluded they contaminate the mean, the bottom
box and the scale length.

### 2.4 The same construct is asked on different scale lengths

`KPLIKE` is a 3-point scale for the 4–6s and a 5-point scale for the 7–12s. Counting boxes
across them manufactures the artefact this study has already published once:

| construct | younger TB | older TB | raw gap | latent gap | verdict |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| funny | 68.0% | 4.8% | **−63.2** | −20.4 | scale artefact |
| exciting | 76.0% | 30.4% | −45.6 | −10.4 | scale artefact |
| scary | 64.0% | 30.4% | −33.6 | −1.5 | scale artefact |
| understood it | 88.0% | 54.4% | −33.6 | — | **option sets differ — not comparable** |

Two genuine age effects survive the correction (funny, exciting) at a fifth to a third of the
apparent size. Three constructs turn out not to be comparable at all: same construct, same
point count, **no shared option wording**.

### 2.5 Ten headline metrics have no closed-end

Overall appeal, appeal to a child, likelihood a child asks to see it, recommend (parent and
non-parent paths), theatrical intent, streaming intent and category interest are all prose.
They cannot enter a table until they are scored, and they are the numbers a distributor cares
about most.

### 2.6 Defects that belong to the export, not the analysis

Worth separating out, because these need fixing upstream rather than handling downstream:

- **Four `TRCONT` questions carry the wrong option list.** The question asks *"too little, the
  right amount, or too much"* and the options supplied are an agree/disagree battery. There is
  no honest ranking of that pairing; the pipeline refuses to produce one.
- **Adult Q33 duplicates Q32** — byte-identical statements, answered identically by 272 of 273
  personas. Reporting both double-counts the battery. (The single disagreement is a free 99.6%
  intra-interview consistency read.)
- **Skip logic was never applied.** All 273 personas answered both the `[PARENT PATH]` and
  `[NON-PARENT PATH]` recommend questions, including the 85 who had just said they are not
  parents. 162 prose answers read *"N/A – I am a parent"*: the personas corrected the base
  themselves, and those rows are counted as evidence about the base rather than as scoring
  failures.
- **`aat_pre_concept_interest_pct` is a cohort fixture**, taking five distinct values across
  273 personas. `aat_interest_delta` is therefore post-interest minus a constant, and is not
  independent evidence of a lift.
- 94–98% of open ends in the prior wave, and 27–93% here, carry roleplay stage directions
  (`[hides face in my shirt]`). Left in, they dominate any vector space and every cluster
  becomes a cluster of gestures.

---

## 3. Architecture

Six layers, and one rule that keeps them honest: **nothing queries raw except staging, and
nothing downstream binds to a single run's table.**

```
GCS  one object per export
 │
 ▼  sp_register_export  — external table, explicit all-STRING schema, provenance kept
abr_01_raw       raw_<run_id>            exact copy of source, immutable
 │
 ▼  sp_unpivot  — schema-driven, generated per export
abr_10_staging   stg_response            one row per persona × question
 │
 ▼
abr_20_curated   dim_run, dim_archetype, dim_aat, dim_question,
                 dim_question_option_scaled, fct_response, fct_response_option
 │
 ▼
abr_30_marts     banner, theme_by_cut, prose_score, mart_run_comparison,
                 known_answer_accuracy, intent_driver, dq_parity
 │
 ▼
abr_40_semantic  embeddings, clusters, and the AI passes — pointed only at the
                 residue the deterministic rules could not settle
```

`abr_00_config` sits beside all of it and holds the **analysis contract**: the intensity
lexicon, the sentinel list, the codeframe, the question roles, the prose rubric. Every judgement
the pipeline makes about what an answer *means* is a row in one of those tables — readable,
diffable, and versioned — rather than a `CASE` expression buried in a query.

### 3.1 Grain and identity

```
dim_run              (run_id)
dim_archetype        (run_id, archetype_id)
dim_question         (run_id, question_key)          question_key is version-stable
dim_question_option  (run_id, question_key, option_raw)
fct_response         (run_id, archetype_id, question_key)
```

Two decisions here carry the whole versioning story:

**`run_id` is on every row, and nothing is ever deduplicated across runs.** Two builds of the
same panel coexist. The difference between them is the measurement, not noise to be collapsed.

**`question_key = hash(panel, meta, question_text)` deliberately excludes build, date and run.**
So the same question in two builds carries the same key and the two are joinable. This is the
single line that makes version testing possible, and adding `build` to it — which looks tidier —
would silently destroy that capability.

### 3.2 Physical design

Clustering only, no partitioning. The whole wave is ~35,000 fact rows; date partitions of a few
hundred rows each would cost more and scan more, not less. Revisit at ~10M rows.

### 3.3 The reshape is generated, not written

`sp_unpivot` reads `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS` for the raw table, finds the `Q{n}_question`
columns, builds one `SELECT` per question block, and executes the union. A channel column absent
in a shorter instrument becomes `NULL` rather than an error. This is the step that cannot be
hand-written once and reused, and it is why "just point BigQuery at the new file" does not
work without it.

The gate is exact: fact rows must equal personas × questions, per run. Anything else raises.

---

## 4. Method: deciding what "top box" means

This is the highest-risk artefact in the build, so it is deterministic, inspectable as rows, and
it refuses to guess quietly.

**Resolution order, per question:**

1. **Printed scale point**, where the label carries one. This is the questionnaire's own scale
   and it wins over the export code.
2. **Intensity lexicon** — 87 phrases, longest match first, so `not at all` beats `at all` and
   `very uncomfortable` beats `very`.
3. **Option code**, last resort, and flagged as unverified.

**Then favourability is derived from intensity plus construct polarity**, because "A lot" is the
best answer to *did you like it* and the worst answer to *was it boring*:

- positive construct → most intense is most favourable
- negative construct (boring, scary, confusing, too long, showed too much) → **least** intense is
  most favourable
- mid-optimal construct (too little / right amount / too much) → distance from the middle

**Nominal questions are not ranked at all.** A wh-question whose options the ladder cannot place
("who would you watch with", "what kind of movie is this") is a pick list. It is reported as
option shares; forcing a rank onto it invents a scale the questionnaire never asked.

**Ranking is dense over distinct scale positions, not over options.** The current wave has a
stray `Neither agree nor disagree` sharing printed point 3 with `To a moderate extent`; ranking
per option would turn a 5-point scale into a 6-point one and move its top box.

**Every option also gets a 0–100 latent favourability score**, which is what allows a 3-point
and a 5-point scale to be compared. Where a label prints its own point, the axis is anchored to
the instrument's full scale (a printed 5 means a 5-point scale) rather than to the options that
happened to be chosen — otherwise an unpicked option stretches the rest and two panels look
further apart than they are.

**Cross-checks that fire automatically:** an option code that does not track intensity, a code
carrying two different labels, an option list that contradicts its question, a lexicon that
covers only part of a scale. In the current wave 5 of 131 closed-ends land in the review queue,
and those 5 — not all 131 — are the only questions the AI pass is asked about.

---

## 5. Method: semantics and themes

Three passes, in an order where each checks the one before.

**Hygiene.** Strip roleplay stage directions (keeping the count, since embodiment is itself a
signal), quarantine generation-harness JSON that leaked into data cells, drop instruction
screens that carry "responses" because the harness answered them anyway, and flag null
responses — *"Nothing, I loved the dog!"* is a null complaint, not a complaint about the dog.
Without that last rule the dislike read shows the dog at 45% and means nothing.

**Codeframe coding.** 24 themes, 190 patterns, multi-label, and every hit records the pattern
that fired so any number traces back to a sentence.

**Emergent clustering with no codeframe at all**, then a coverage check: clusters the frame
barely touches are reported as gaps. This is the pass that finds the theme nobody thought to
seed. In the prior wave it was an audio/sensory complaint volunteered by 40%+ of personas that
no closed-end option anywhere could capture. In this wave it surfaced adults praising that the
trailer *"tells you exactly what you're getting"* — clarity as a positive, which correlates
**with** intent while predictability correlates **against** it. Collapsing the two would have
cancelled a real finding.

**Incidence is scoped to a question role.** This is the difference between a number and a
decoration. "Does this persona mention the dog anywhere across 20 open ends and 13 diagnostic
prose fields" is ~100% for every theme worth having. Questions are grouped by the read they
support — first reaction, likes, unprompted dislikes, scary probe, comprehension, recall, intent
— and incidence is per persona *within* a role, on a base of personas who answered a question in
that role, with the null-response rate beside it.

---

## 6. Validation without a human benchmark

There is no human trailer test for this title. The usual calibration route is closed. Four
routes remain, and they are the methodological core of this paper.

### 6.1 Known-answer accuracy

Some questions have a checkable right answer. The trailer said theatrical, and it said
January 22, 2027.

| Panel | Question | Fact | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Adults | `RETITLE` | title is *Air Bud Returns* | 100.0% (273/273) |
| Adults | `DRELEASE` | release January 22, 2027 | 99.6% (272/273) |
| Adults | `DLOC` | in theatres first | 100.0% (273/273) |
| Kids 7–12 | `KPRSE` | in theatres first | 100.0% (125/125) |
| Kids 4–6 | `KPRSE` | in theatres first | 96.0% (24/25) |

Stimulus comprehension is essentially perfect. **What needs an anchor is the level of the
panel's evaluations, not its grasp of what it saw.**

### 6.2 Replication across independently generated runs

31 of the 4–6 panel's 36 questions and 39 of the 7–12 panel's 40 are worded identically to the
prior wave's exports, on **disjoint personas**. That is an independent re-run of the same
instrument — which the prior wave's own documentation recorded as *unmeasured*, because nothing
in it was a replicate.

| Pair | Matched constructs | Rank-order ρ | Mean abs. latent Δ | Largest move |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Kids 7–12 ↔ prior | 19 | 0.691 | **8.8 pts** | scary/upsetting, 94.8 → 75.8 |
| Kids 4–6 ↔ prior | 14 | 0.530 | **5.9 pts** | title liking, 74.4 → 92.0 |

**This is a caution, not a pass.** Rank order survives moderately well, which supports
rank-based reporting. Levels do not: a mean absolute movement of 6–9 latent points between two
runs of one instrument means every single-run level carries at least that much run-to-run
uncertainty *on top of* its sampling interval, and no confidence interval in the banner accounts
for it. The constructs that moved most — scary/upsetting, title liking, kids-and-grown-ups-both-
enjoy — are the least safe to quote from one run.

A cleaner floor is available and worth generating deliberately: the **same build, generated
twice**. The pipeline classifies such a pair as a `replicate` and reports its empirical floor
automatically; there is not one in the data yet.

### 6.3 Triangulation on the prose metrics

The prose metrics are scored twice independently — once by a written rubric, once by the
generator's own `aat_*` verdict on the same construct — and optionally a third time by a model.

| Metric | Rubric top box | Agreement with `aat_*` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Overall appeal | 76.1% | **98.2%** |
| Theatrical intent | 56.5% | **75.3%** |

Two independent readings agreeing is evidence. Disagreeing is a finding: appeal is being read
the same way by both routes, and theatrical intent — the commercially decisive number — is not.
That is where a third opinion is worth paying for, and it is the one place the AI pass is
pointed first.

### 6.4 Parity between implementations

The pipeline exists twice: as a reference implementation in dependency-free Python, and as
BigQuery SQL. Nineteen measured anchors from the reference run — row counts, specific top-box
percentages, specific theme incidences — are asserted against the warehouse output in
`abr_30_marts.dq_parity`, and the run fails on a mismatch. Two independent implementations of
the same rules agreeing on nineteen specific numbers is a stronger statement about the rules
than either implementation makes alone.

---

## 7. What this wave says about the film

Reported here only to show the method producing readable output; every figure carries its base
and its interval in `abr_30_marts.banner`.

**Adults.** Comfort letting a child see it, 90.1% top box (n=273). Easy to understand and
clearly introduced characters both above 93%. Appeal 76.1% top box, theatrical intent 56.5%.

**What travels with theatrical intent** (rank correlation, direction and ordering only — n=273
with demographics balanced by design, so neither a causal nor a significance reading applies):

| ρ | feature |
|---:|---|
| **+0.744** | "worth seeing on a large movie-theatre screen" |
| +0.602 | "enjoyable for both children and adults" |
| +0.553 | "feels unique and different from other family movies" |
| **−0.406** | mentions predictable / formulaic |
| **−0.343** | mentions cost / ticket price |

Both detractors are addressable in marketing rather than in the film.

**Children, unprompted dislikes.** The clown animal-control officer is the largest volunteered
negative in the study and it lands hardest on the youngest: **22 of 25** of the 4–6s raised it
unprompted, 59.2% of the 7–12s, 42.9% of adults. Among the 7–12s who reached the scary probe it
appears in 100% of answers. Sad or upsetting moments: 52% of the 4–6s. The audio/sensory theme
recurs across all open ends at 46.5% of adults, 40.0% of the 4–6s and 33.6% of the 7–12s — and
remains invisible to the closed-ends, because no option in this questionnaire captures sound
load.

---

## 8. Limitations

- **Percentages on a base of 25 are not percentages.** The 4–6 panel is read as counts. 969 of
  1,508 banner cells fall below n=30 and every one carries a flag.
- **Absolute levels are unanchored.** §6 buys rank order, replication and known-answer accuracy.
  It does not buy a calibrated level, and no amount of internal validation will.
- **Run-to-run variance is not in any interval.** §6.2 measures it at 6–9 latent points; the
  Wilson intervals in the banner do not include it. Both numbers belong on any published figure.
- **Scale length is bounded by the observed option universe.** Where a label prints its own
  point the full instrument scale is recoverable; elsewhere an option nobody chose is invisible
  and slightly compresses the latent axis.
- **The deterministic passes are baselines with known coverage.** 5 of 131 closed-ends unresolved;
  75% of applicable prose scored; 88% of verbatims coded. All three shortfalls are enumerated in
  review files rather than absorbed.
- **Correlations are hypothesis generators.** Stated again because it is the easiest sentence in
  a deck to drop.
- **A codeframe is a hypothesis.** §5's clustering pass is the check on it, and it has already
  found one gap in this wave. It will find more.

---

## 9. Running it

**In BigQuery (Cloud Shell).** Everything, no Python analysis step:

```bash
./bq/run_bq.sh -p PROJECT -b BUCKET -d /path/to/exports
```

Stages: datasets and config → UDFs → register and unpivot each export → curated → scale map →
themes → prose → marts → the data-quality gate. `--ai` adds the four optional AI stages;
`--dry-run` prints the plan without touching the project. Adding a version later is the same
command with the new file in the folder.

**As the reference implementation** (any machine with `python3`, no dependencies, ~23 seconds
on the full wave):

```bash
./run_all.sh /path/to/exports
```

**Adding a version by hand**, if you would rather not use the driver:

```sql
CALL `PROJECT.abr_00_config.sp_register_export`(
  'gs://BUCKET/abr/v2/htr_k9_43p_1_0.csv', 'htr_k9_43p_1_0',
  'HTR_K9',            -- the SAME panel code as the earlier build. This is what
                       -- makes the two joinable in mart_run_comparison.
  'HTR', '43p.1.0', '10-15', 1);
CALL `PROJECT.abr_00_config.sp_unpivot`('htr_k9_43p_1_0');
-- then re-run 04 through 09
```

**Reading the results, in this order:**

```sql
SELECT * FROM `PROJECT.abr_30_marts.dq_parity` ORDER BY status DESC;        -- is it right?
SELECT * FROM `PROJECT.abr_20_curated.dim_question_review`;                 -- what is unresolved?
SELECT * FROM `PROJECT.abr_30_marts.mart_run_agreement`;                    -- how much noise?
SELECT * FROM `PROJECT.abr_30_marts.banner` WHERE cut = 'total';            -- the numbers
SELECT * FROM `PROJECT.abr_30_marts.mart_run_comparison` WHERE verdict = 'material';
```

The order is deliberate. The first two questions are whether the pipeline is right and what it
could not settle; the third is how much movement is meaningless. Only then the numbers.

---

## Appendix A — the analysis contract

Four config tables hold every judgement about meaning. Edit the JSON in `conf/`, regenerate with
`python3 tools/gen_bq_config.py > bq/01_config.sql`, and commit both.

| Table | Rows | What it decides |
|---|---:|---|
| `scale_intensity` | 87 | The intensity ladder for option labels |
| `scale_sentinel` | 19 | Which options sit outside the scale |
| `construct_polarity` | 14 | Which questions invert favourability |
| `nominal_meta` | 36 | Which questions are pick lists, not scales |
| `codeframe` | 190 | The themes, and the patterns that trigger them |
| `question_role` | 26 | Which questions support which read |
| `prose_cue` | 38 | The rubric for scoring prose onto a 5-point scale |

Patterns must be RE2-safe — no lookahead, no lookbehind, no backreferences. The generator
rejects anything that is not, rather than letting it fail at query time.

## Appendix B — what to change when a new instrument arrives

| Change | What it costs |
|---|---|
| A new build of an existing panel | Nothing. One `CALL` pair, then rebuild. |
| A new panel in an existing instrument | Nothing. Same. |
| New question wording for an existing construct | It stops matching across runs, deliberately. Decide whether it is the same question. |
| New option labels the lexicon does not know | The question lands in the review queue. Add the phrases to `scale_intensity`. |
| A new theme | Add it to `codeframe`; re-run stage 6. Prior runs are re-coded consistently. |
| A prompt change in an AI stage | **Re-codes the whole study.** Version the prompt with the run, or two builds become incomparable for reasons unrelated to the film. |
